title: Is Classroom Management Icky? And Does It Even Matter for This Fall?
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Prompted by a conversation with Lynsay Fabio, co-author of his Classroom Management Course, Stuart addresses teachers who instinctively recoil from the term "classroom management" as crude or coercive. He argues that understanding and shaping group behavior toward productive ends isn't inherently brutish — done well, it mixes authority with warmth and is the difference between "hating your job as a teacher and loving it." He contends classroom management is a learnable, transferable skill set rather than an intuition some teachers simply lack, built from concrete principles like "authoritative presence," the deliberate use of body, voice, and word choice. Anticipating a possible shift to remote instruction in the fall, he tests whether these skills still matter outside a physical classroom by reviewing his own remote-teaching videos, and concludes they do, since the same deliberate use of presence and voice carried over directly to video instruction.
points: Stuart directly names and reframes teachers' discomfort with the word "management," arguing the underlying skill — not the label — determines whether classroom stewardship feels like coercion or care.
His key claim is that classroom management is a masterable, transferable skill set, not an innate gift some teachers have and others lack.
He introduces "authoritative presence" — deliberate use of body, voice, and word choice — as a concrete, practicable component of classroom management.
He tests his own claims against the pandemic's shift to remote teaching and concludes the underlying skills of presence, voice, and word choice transfer directly to video instruction.
quotes: Now, a percentage of teachers, when they see the term "classroom management" or the phrase "managing behavior," wrinkle their noses and they think, "Ugh… how Cro-magnon! Who are we to think that it's our job to manage student behavior?

Listen: understanding how group behavior works and how to shape it toward productive ends isn't crude or brutish or coercive. It's the difference between hating your job as a teacher and loving it; it turns frustration into flourishing.

I can still picture the card table that stood in my apartment's kitchen during my first year of teaching. I would sit down at that table some nights and literally pray through my class rosters, covered with the highlighted names of children I couldn't seem to get to listen to me.
There are ways of using your body and your voice that draw human attention, and every human can understand and physically practice these things until they become automatic.

And shortly after that, I went and made a brief instructional video for one of my classes. I found myself thinking afresh about my body, my voice, and my choice of words. Does authoritative presence matter when we're teaching students remotely? Yes.
